title: Ἀχιλλέως ψυχή
titleEn: Agamemnon’s Warning, Achilles’ Soul and News of Neoptolemus — Odyssey 11.435–537
part: Agamemnon’s Warning, Achilles’ Soul and News of Neoptolemus (11.435–537)
about: Odysseus, still telling the Phaeacians of the underworld, answers Agamemnon with a cry that the house of Atreus has always suffered through women. Agamemnon replies with a warning: never be gentle with a woman or tell her everything, and bring your ship home in secret, though Penelope, he grants, is discerning and will not do as Clytemnestra did. He asks for news of his son Orestes, and Odysseus has none. As the two stand weeping, the souls of Achilles, Patroclus, Antilochus and Ajax come up. Achilles asks how Odysseus could bring himself to come down among the dead. Odysseus says he came to consult Tiresias, calls Achilles the most blessed of men, honoured in life and a ruler among the dead. Achilles answers that he would rather be a hired hand on earth than lord over the dead, and asks for news of his son and of his father Peleus. Odysseus knows nothing of Peleus but tells of Neoptolemus: how he spoke first in counsel, fought far in front of the host, killed Eurypylus, and sat in the wooden horse without a tear or a tremor, begging to be let out, and how he sailed home unwounded after the sack of Troy.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
sentences.n: The formula that introduces a reply, here Odysseus answering Agamemnon, whose speech ended at line 434. ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (ἔφατ’ is ἔφατο elided, unaugmented), ἀμειβόμενος ‘answering’ and προσέειπον ‘I addressed’, the first-person form. The English is kept exactly as when this line was shipped before, where the speaker was a woman; μιν is ‘him’ or ‘her’ in Greek, so read ‘she … her’ as ‘he … him’, for Agamemnon is the speaker.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι, ἦ μάλα δὴ γόνον Ἀτρέος εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς
ἐκπάγλως ἤχθηρε γυναικείας διὰ βουλὰς
ἐξ ἀρχῆς·
sentences.i: ‘Ah, truly Zeus who thunders from afar has hated the offspring of Atreus terribly from the beginning, because of the plans of women;
sentences.n: Odysseus’ cry of dismay at what he has just heard. ὢ πόποι is ‘Ah’, ἦ μάλα δή ‘truly, very much’, and γόνον Ἀτρέος ‘the offspring of Atreus’, the family of Atreus as the object of Zeus’s hatred. ἤχθηρε is the aorist of ἐχθαίρω ‘hate’, and ἐκπάγλως ‘terribly, exceedingly’. εὐρύοπα Ζεύς is the traditional ‘Zeus who thunders from afar’; the second element, from ὄψ, may be ‘voice’ or ‘eye, face’, so the sense is disputed. γυναικείας διὰ βουλάς is ‘because of the plans of women’ (διά with the accusative), and ἐξ ἀρχῆς ‘from the beginning’. The ano teleia ends the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t:
Ἑλένης μὲν ἀπωλόμεθ’ εἵνεκα πολλοί,
σοὶ δὲ Κλυταιμνήστρη δόλον ἤρτυε τηλόθ’ ἐόντι.
sentences.l:
for Helen’s sake, indeed, we perished, many of us,
but for you Clytemnestra a trick prepared, you being far away.’
sentences.i: Many of us perished for Helen’s sake, but for you Clytemnestra prepared a trick while you were far away.’
sentences.n: The two women named. Ἑλένης … εἵνεκα is ‘for the sake of Helen’ (εἵνεκα follows its noun), ἀπωλόμεθ’ the aorist middle of ἀπόλλυμι ‘we perished’, and πολλοί ‘many’. σοὶ δέ answers the μέν: ‘but for you’. Κλυταιμνήστρη is Clytemnestra; δόλον ἤρτυε is ‘was preparing a trick’ (ἀρτύω ‘fit together, prepare’, imperfect), and τηλόθ’ ἐόντι is ‘while you were far off’, a dative participle agreeing with σοί. Odysseus’ speech ends.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δέ μ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπε·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and he then at once, answering me, addressed me:
sentences.i: So I said, and he answered me at once:
sentences.n: Agamemnon’s reply-formula, the same line as 11.404 in the previous part: ὣς ἐφάμην ‘so I spoke’, ὁ δέ ‘and he’ (the old pronoun use of the article), αὐτίκ’ ‘at once’, ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπε ‘answering addressed’. The English is as shipped.

sentences.t: τῷ νῦν μή ποτε καὶ σὺ γυναικί περ ἤπιος εἶναι·
sentences.l: ‘Therefore now never you too, even to a woman, be kind:
sentences.i: ‘So now, you too, never be gentle, even to a woman:
sentences.n: Agamemnon’s advice begins. τῷ is ‘therefore’, and μή ποτε … εἶναι is an infinitive doing the work of a command, ‘never be …’; the next lines go on in the same way (πιφαυσκέμεν, φάσθαι, κατισχέμεναι). ἤπιος is ‘kind, gentle’ (the house gives ‘kind’ in the literal layer and ‘gentle’ in the other), καὶ σύ ‘you too’, and περ after γυναικί ‘even’. γυνή means both ‘woman’ and ‘wife’; the next lines are plainly about Penelope, but the Greek says ‘a woman’, and the English keeps that.

sentences.t:
μή οἱ μῦθον ἅπαντα πιφαυσκέμεν, ὅν κ’ ἐὺ εἰδῇς,
ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν φάσθαι, τὸ δὲ καὶ κεκρυμμένον εἶναι.
sentences.l:
not to her the whole tale to disclose, whichever you may know well,
but the one part to say, and the other even hidden to be.
sentences.i: do not disclose to her the whole of any tale that you know well, but tell her one part, and let the other be kept hidden.
sentences.n: What he is to hold back. πιφαυσκέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν (πιφαύσκω ‘make known, declare’) still serving as a command after μή, and οἱ is ‘to her’. ὅν κ’ ἐὺ εἰδῇς is ‘whichever tale you know well’: ὅν κε with the subjunctive of οἶδα makes a general relative clause, and ἐύ is εὖ ‘well’. τὸ μὲν φάσθαι, τὸ δὲ … is ‘the one to say, the other …’, with the article τό as a pronoun and φάσθαι the infinitive of the middle of φημί. κεκρυμμένον εἶναι is ‘to be hidden’, a perfect passive participle with εἶναι. μῦθος is ‘tale’ here.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐ σοί γ’, Ὀδυσεῦ, φόνος ἔσσεται ἔκ γε γυναικός·
sentences.l: But not for you, Odysseus, will slaughter be from a woman;
sentences.i: But for you, Odysseus, there will be no murder at a woman’s hand;
sentences.n: The reassurance. ἀλλ’ οὐ σοί γ’ is ‘but not for you’, and Ὀδυσεῦ is the vocative of Ὀδυσσεύς in its single-σ spelling, which the poet may use as the metre requires. ἔσσεται is ἔσται ‘will be’ with the doubled σ of epic, and φόνος is ‘murder, slaughter’. ἔκ γε γυναικός is literally ‘from a woman’, that is, at a woman’s hand.

sentences.t:
λίην γὰρ πινυτή τε καὶ εὖ φρεσὶ μήδεα οἶδε
κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο, περίφρων Πηνελόπεια.
sentences.l:
for exceedingly discerning she is, and well in her mind counsels she knows,
the daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope.
sentences.i: for she is exceedingly discerning, and well versed in counsels in her mind, the daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope.
sentences.n: Why Penelope is different. λίην is ‘exceedingly’, πινυτή ‘discerning’ (the adjective belongs with πεπνυμένος, the word used of Telemachus, but the house keeps the two apart: ‘discerning’ here, ‘prudent’ there), and εὖ φρεσὶ μήδεα οἶδε is ‘knows counsels well in her mind’, that is, is skilled in planning. κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο is ‘the daughter of Icarius’ with the genitive -οιο, and περίφρων Πηνελόπεια ‘circumspect Penelope’, the epithet as it stands in the same line elsewhere in the poem, with Πηνελόπεια the epic form of the name.

sentences.t:
ἦ μέν μιν νύμφην γε νέην κατελείπομεν ἡμεῖς
ἐρχόμενοι πόλεμόνδε·
sentences.l:
Truly her, a bride, young, we left behind, we ourselves,
going to the war;
sentences.i: Truly, we left her behind as a young bride when we went off to the war;
sentences.n: The child she was left with. ἦ μέν is ‘truly’, νύμφη ‘bride, young wife’, νέην ‘young’, and κατελείπομεν ‘we were leaving’, the imperfect of καταλείπω, with ἡμεῖς ‘we ourselves’ for emphasis. ἐρχόμενοι πόλεμόνδε is ‘going to the war’, with the -δε of direction. The ano teleia ends the unit in mid-line; the clause about the child begins on the rest of the line.

sentences.t:
πάϊς δέ οἱ ἦν ἐπὶ μαζῷ
νήπιος, ὅς που νῦν γε μετ’ ἀνδρῶν ἵζει ἀριθμῷ,
ὄλβιος·
sentences.i: and at her breast was an infant son, who now, I think, takes his place in the count of men, a prosperous one;
sentences.n: Telemachus, who is not named: ‘a child’. πάϊς is the epic form of παῖς, ἐπὶ μαζῷ is ‘at the breast’, and νήπιος here means ‘infant’, literally ‘not speaking’ (the house keeps ‘foolish’ for the same word of a grown man; here that would make no sense). ὅς που … ἵζει is ‘who, I suppose, now sits’, with που ‘somewhere, I suppose’, and μετ’ ἀνδρῶν ἀριθμῷ is ‘in the number of men’, that is, is counted among grown men. ὄλβιος is ‘prosperous’, the house word, and is explained by the next line. The unit ends at the ano teleia after ὄλβιος, in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἦ γὰρ τόν γε πατὴρ φίλος ὄψεται ἐλθών,
καὶ κεῖνος πατέρα προσπτύξεται, ἣ θέμις ἐστίν.
sentences.l:
for truly him his dear father will see, having come,
and that one his father will embrace, as is right.
sentences.i: For his dear father will come and see him, and he in turn will embrace his father, as is right.
sentences.n: Why the child is fortunate. ἦ γάρ is ‘for truly’, τόν γε ‘him’, πατὴρ φίλος ‘his dear father’, and ὄψεται ἐλθών ‘will see, on coming’ (ὄψεται future of ὁράω). καὶ κεῖνος is ‘and that one’ (κεῖνος = ἐκεῖνος), προσπτύξεται ‘will embrace’ (literally ‘will fold to himself’), and ἣ θέμις ἐστίν ‘as is right’: ἣ is the adverb ‘as, in the way that’ (ᾗ), and θέμις ‘what is established, right’.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἐμὴ οὐδέ περ υἷος ἐνιπλησθῆναι ἄκοιτις
ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἔασε·
sentences.l:
But mine, not even of a son to be filled, my wife
with the eyes allowed;
sentences.i: But my wife did not even let me take my fill of my son with my eyes;
sentences.n: Clytemnestra’s denial. ἡ δ’ ἐμὴ … ἄκοιτις is ‘but my wife’ (ἄκοιτις is ‘bedfellow, wife’), and ἔασε is the aorist of ἐάω ‘allow’. ἐνιπλησθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of ἐμπίμπλημι ‘fill’, ‘to be filled’, with the genitive υἷος ‘of a son’ (to take one’s fill of the sight) and ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ‘with the eyes’; the Greek has no ‘my’ with υἷος and no ‘me’, and the English supplies both. The ano teleia ends the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t: πάρος δέ με πέφνε καὶ αὐτόν.
sentences.l: but before, me she killed, even myself.
sentences.i: but before that she killed me myself as well.
sentences.n: πάρος is ‘before (that)’, and με … καὶ αὐτόν is ‘me, even myself’: she killed him first, before he could look at his son. πέφνε is the unaugmented aorist of the root φεν- ‘kill’ (the usual aorist is ἔπεφνον); Homer’s past tenses need not take the augment.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσιν·
sentences.l: And another thing to you I will say, and you in your own mind lay it:
sentences.i: And I will tell you something else; lay it up in your own mind:
sentences.n: Agamemnon’s second piece of advice. ἄλλο is ‘another thing’, ἐρέω is the epic future of ἐρῶ ‘I will say’, and τοι is σοι ‘to you’. βάλλεο is the imperative of the middle βάλλομαι ‘put, lay for oneself’, with ἐνὶ φρεσὶ … σῇσιν ‘in your own mind’ (σῇσιν the dative plural of σός ‘your’, agreeing with φρεσί).

sentences.t:
κρύβδην, μηδ’ ἀναφανδά, φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν
νῆα κατισχέμεναι·
sentences.l:
secretly, and not openly, to your dear fatherland
the ship to bring in;
sentences.i: bring your ship in to your dear fatherland secretly, and not openly;
sentences.n: The advice itself, in infinitives that serve as commands. κρύβδην ‘secretly’ and ἀναφανδά ‘openly’ are adverbs, joined by μηδ’ ‘and not’. φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν is ‘to your dear fatherland’ (the Greek has no ‘your’), and νῆα κατισχέμεναι is ‘to bring the ship in’: κατίσχω is ‘hold down’, said of bringing a ship to land, here in an infinitive in -έμεναι. The ano teleia ends the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t: ἐπεὶ οὐκέτι πιστὰ γυναιξίν.
sentences.l: since no longer (is anything) trustworthy with women.
sentences.i: for there is no longer any trust to be put in women.
sentences.n: The reason. ἐπεί is ‘since’, οὐκέτι ‘no longer’, and πιστά ‘trustworthy things’, neuter plural, with γυναιξίν the dative plural ‘with women’. There is no verb, so the sense is ‘nothing is any longer to be trusted with women’; that is, women can no longer be trusted.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον,
εἴ που ἔτι ζώοντος ἀκούετε παιδὸς ἐμοῖο,
ἤ που ἐν Ὀρχομενῷ ἢ ἐν Πύλῳ ἠμαθόεντι,
ἤ που πὰρ Μενελάῳ ἐνὶ Σπάρτῃ εὐρείῃ·
sentences.l:
But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly,
whether anywhere, still living, you hear of my child,
perhaps in Orchomenus or in sandy Pylos,
or perhaps beside Menelaus in broad Sparta;
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly, whether you have heard anywhere that my son is still alive, perhaps in Orchomenus or in sandy Pylos, or perhaps with Menelaus in broad Sparta;
sentences.n: Agamemnon turns to his own question, about Orestes. The first line is the formula ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον ‘but come, tell me this, and recount it exactly’, in the same English as before, but with a comma because the question follows. εἴ που … ἀκούετε is ‘whether anywhere you hear’: εἰ introduces an indirect question, and ἀκούετε is plural, ‘you’ meaning the living. ζώοντος παιδὸς ἐμοῖο is a genitive after ἀκούω, ‘hear of my child living’. ἤ που … ἢ … ἤ που is ‘perhaps … or … or perhaps’; Ὀρχομενῷ is Orchomenus (the poem does not say which town of that name), Πύλῳ ἠμαθόεντι ‘sandy Pylos’, and Σπάρτῃ εὐρείῃ ‘broad Sparta’, with εὐρείῃ the Ionic feminine of εὐρύς and πὰρ Μενελάῳ ‘beside Menelaus’.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ πω τέθνηκεν ἐπὶ χθονὶ δῖος Ὀρέστης.
sentences.l: for not yet has he died on the earth, heavenly Orestes.’
sentences.i: for heavenly Orestes has not yet died on the earth.’
sentences.n: The reason for the question. οὐ γάρ πω τέθνηκεν is ‘for he has not yet died’ (τέθνηκεν the perfect of θνῄσκω), ἐπὶ χθονί ‘on the earth’ (dative of χθών), and δῖος Ὀρέστης ‘heavenly Orestes’, with the house ‘heavenly’ for δῖος. Agamemnon’s speech ends here, and Murray’s next paragraph returns to Odysseus.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
sentences.n: The formula again, now before Odysseus’ answer about Orestes. The English is kept exactly as when this line was shipped before, where the speaker was a woman; μιν is ‘him’ or ‘her’ in Greek, so read ‘she … her’ as ‘he … him’, for Agamemnon is the speaker.

sentences.t: Ἀτρεΐδη, τί με ταῦτα διείρεαι;
sentences.l: ‘Son of Atreus, why do you ask me these things?
sentences.i: ‘Son of Atreus, why do you ask me this?
sentences.n: Odysseus has no news. Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative of Ἀτρεΐδης, the patronymic ‘son of Atreus’ used as a form of address. τί με ταῦτα διείρεαι is ‘why do you ask me these things?’: διείρομαι ‘ask, question’ takes two accusatives, με and ταῦτα. The Greek question mark ends the unit after διείρεαι, in mid-line.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι οἶδα,
ζώει ὅ γ’ ἦ τέθνηκε·
sentences.l:
and I do not know at all,
lives he, or has he died;
sentences.i: I do not know at all whether he is alive or dead;
sentences.n: οὐδέ τι οἶδα is ‘and I know nothing’ (τι an adverb ‘at all’, οἶδα ‘I know’). ζώει ὅ γ’ ἦ τέθνηκε is the alternative itself, ‘lives he, or has he died’, an indirect question with no introducing word: ὅ γε is ‘he’ (the article as a pronoun, with emphatic γε), ἦ is ‘or’, and τέθνηκε the perfect ‘has died’. The ano teleia ends the unit before the proverb.

sentences.t: κακὸν δ’ ἀνεμώλια βάζειν.
sentences.l: and bad it is windy things to speak.’
sentences.i: and it is bad to speak empty words.’
sentences.n: A proverb-like close. κακόν is ‘bad’ with ἐστί understood, ἀνεμώλια ‘windy’, hence ‘empty, idle’ (from ἄνεμος ‘wind’), and βάζειν ‘to speak, chatter’. Odysseus’ speech ends.

sentences.t:
νῶι μὲν ὣς ἐπέεσσιν ἀμειβομένω στυγεροῖσιν
ἕσταμεν ἀχνύμενοι θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυ χέοντες·
sentences.l:
We two thus, with words exchanging, hateful,
stood, grieving, an abundant tear shedding;
sentences.i: So we two stood exchanging hateful words, grieving and shedding abundant tears;
sentences.n: Murray’s new paragraph: the two men stand talking and weeping. The first line stands elsewhere in the poem, and its English follows that earlier wording; the second line is new. νῶι is the dual ‘we two’ and ἀμειβομένω the dual participle ‘exchanging’, with ἐπέεσσιν στυγεροῖσιν ‘with hateful words’ (the -εσσι dative). ἕσταμεν is ‘we stood’, the perfect of ἵστημι in the form -μεν (Attic ἑστήκαμεν), and ἀχνύμενοι ‘grieving’. θαλερὸν … δάκρυ χέοντες is ‘shedding an abundant tear’: the house renders θαλερός as ‘abundant’, and the singular δάκρυ is collective, ‘tears’.

sentences.t:
ἦλθε δ’ ἐπὶ ψυχὴ Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος
καὶ Πατροκλῆος καὶ ἀμύμονος Ἀντιλόχοιο
Αἴαντός θ’, ὃς ἄριστος ἔην εἶδός τε δέμας τε
τῶν ἄλλων Δαναῶν μετ’ ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα.
sentences.l:
And came next the soul of Achilles, Peleus’ son,
and of Patroclus and of blameless Antilochus,
and of Ajax, who was best in form and in body
of the other Danaans, after the blameless son of Peleus.
sentences.i: Next there came the soul of Achilles, son of Peleus, and of Patroclus, and of blameless Antilochus, and of Ajax, who was the best in form and build of the other Greeks, after the blameless son of Peleus.
sentences.n: More souls arrive. ἦλθε δ’ ἐπί is ‘and there came next’, ἐπί being an adverb here. ψυχή governs a string of genitives, and the singular verb agrees with the first name only: Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος is ‘of Achilles, son of Peleus’ (a patronymic with the epic genitive -εω), Πατροκλῆος ‘of Patroclus’, ἀμύμονος Ἀντιλόχοιο ‘of blameless Antilochus’, and Αἴαντός θ’ ‘and of Ajax’. ἀμύμων is kept as ‘blameless’ in every use; what it first meant is not known, and the house word is a convention, not a claim that these men were without fault. ὃς ἄριστος ἔην is ‘who was best’ (ἔην = ἦν) in εἶδός τε δέμας τε ‘form and body’ (accusatives of respect), τῶν ἄλλων Δαναῶν ‘of the other Danaans’, μετ’ ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα ‘next after the blameless son of Peleus’, that is, after Achilles, named here by his father.

sentences.t:
ἔγνω δὲ ψυχή με ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο
καί ῥ’ ὀλοφυρομένη ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And knew me the soul of the swift-footed descendant of Aeacus,
and, lamenting, winged words spoke:
sentences.i: And the soul of the swift-footed descendant of Aeacus recognized me and, lamenting, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: Achilles’ soul speaks. ἔγνω is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘recognized’, with ψυχή the subject and με the object. ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο is ‘of the swift-footed descendant of Aeacus’: Αἰακίδης is the patronymic from Aeacus, the father of Peleus, so it names Achilles, and ποδώκης is ‘swift-footed’ (πούς ‘foot’ and ὠκύς ‘swift’). ὀλοφυρομένη ‘lamenting’ is feminine only because ψυχή is a feminine noun, so the English does not say ‘she’. καί ῥ’ is ‘and then’, and ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the formula ‘spoke winged words’ (προσηύδα, imperfect of προσαυδάω).

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ,
σχέτλιε, τίπτ’ ἔτι μεῖζον ἐνὶ φρεσὶ μήσεαι ἔργον;
sentences.l:
‘Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
Cruel one, why still a greater deed in your mind will you devise?
sentences.i: ‘Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, cruel one, why will you still devise a greater deed in your mind?
sentences.n: Achilles’ words open with a vocative line used elsewhere in the poem: διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ ‘Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices’ (Λαερτιάδη is the patronymic). σχέτλιε is ‘cruel one’ in the house rendering; the word is said of a man who goes too far, ‘hard, reckless’. τίπτ’ is τί ποτε ‘why ever’, μεῖζον … ἔργον ‘a greater deed’, and μήσεαι the future of μήδομαι ‘devise’, with the uncontracted -εαι. The Greek question mark ends the unit.

sentences.t:
πῶς ἔτλης Ἄϊδόσδε κατελθέμεν, ἔνθα τε νεκροὶ
ἀφραδέες ναίουσι, βροτῶν εἴδωλα καμόντων;
sentences.l:
How did you bring yourself to go down to Hades, where the dead
senseless dwell, phantoms of mortals who have toiled?’
sentences.i: How did you bring yourself to go down to Hades, where the dead dwell senseless, phantoms of mortals whose toil is done?’
sentences.n: πῶς ἔτλης is ‘how did you bring yourself’ (ἔτλης the aorist of τλάω ‘endure, bring oneself to’); Ἄϊδόσδε is ‘to Hades’ with the -δε of direction, and κατελθέμεν the infinitive ‘to go down’ (Attic κατελθεῖν). ἀφραδέες is ‘senseless’ (ἀ- and φράζομαι ‘think, understand’): the dead have no wits. βροτῶν εἴδωλα καμόντων is ‘phantoms of mortals who have toiled’: εἴδωλον is ‘phantom’, and καμόντων the aorist participle of κάμνω ‘toil, grow weary’, a gentle word for the dead, ‘those whose toil is done’. Achilles’ speech ends at the question mark.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
sentences.n: The formula, here before Odysseus’ reply to Achilles. The English is kept exactly as when this line was shipped before, where the speaker was a woman; μιν is ‘him’ or ‘her’ in Greek, so read ‘she … her’ as ‘he … him’, for Achilles is the speaker.

sentences.t:
ὦ Ἀχιλεῦ Πηλῆος υἱέ, μέγα φέρτατ’ Ἀχαιῶν,
ἦλθον Τειρεσίαο κατὰ χρέος, εἴ τινα βουλὴν
εἴποι, ὅπως Ἰθάκην ἐς παιπαλόεσσαν ἱκοίμην·
sentences.i: ‘O Achilles, son of Peleus, by far the best of the Achaeans, I came because I had need of Tiresias, to see whether he would tell me some plan by which I might reach rugged Ithaca;
sentences.n: Why Odysseus is in the underworld. ὦ Ἀχιλεῦ Πηλῆος υἱέ is ‘O Achilles, son of Peleus’ (Πηλῆος the epic genitive), and μέγα φέρτατ’ Ἀχαιῶν ‘by far the best of the Achaeans’: φέρτατος is the superlative of the adjective from the root of φέρω, ‘best, mightiest’, and Ἀχαιῶν a partitive genitive. ἦλθον Τειρεσίαο κατὰ χρέος is ‘I came for need of Tiresias’: χρέος is ‘need, business’, and the genitive names the man he needed. εἴ τινα βουλὴν εἴποι is ‘whether he would tell some plan’, an optative in an indirect question after a past verb, and ὅπως … ἱκοίμην ‘how I might reach’. Ἰθάκην ἐς παιπαλόεσσαν is ‘to rugged Ithaca’; the sense of παιπαλόεσσα is not certain beyond ‘rugged, rocky’, and the house keeps ‘rugged’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πω σχεδὸν ἦλθον Ἀχαιΐδος, οὐδέ πω ἁμῆς
γῆς ἐπέβην, ἀλλ’ αἰὲν ἔχω κακά.
sentences.l:
for not yet near the Achaean land have I come, nor yet on our
land have I set foot, but ever I have ills.
sentences.i: For I have not yet come near the Achaean land, nor set foot on any land of ours, but I always have ills.
sentences.n: Odysseus has not yet been home. The first line and a half are the words of an earlier speech in the poem, and their English is kept; the ending is new. οὐ γάρ πω is ‘for not yet’, and Ἀχαιΐδος … γῆς ‘the Achaean land’ (Ἀχαιΐς is a feminine adjective). ἁμῆς is ‘our’, an old form of ἡμετέρης, so ‘our own land’ means Ithaca. ἐπέβην is the aorist of ἐπιβαίνω ‘set foot on’, αἰὲν the epic form of αἰεί ‘always’, and ἔχω κακά ‘I have ills’. The full stop falls in mid-line, and the rest of the line starts the next unit.

sentences.t:
σεῖο δ’, Ἀχιλλεῦ,
οὔ τις ἀνὴρ προπάροιθε μακάρτατος οὔτ’ ἄρ’ ὀπίσσω.
sentences.l:
but of you, Achilles,
no man before was most blessed, nor yet after.
sentences.i: But no man before you has been more blessed than you, Achilles, and none will be after.
sentences.n: Praise of Achilles. σεῖο is the epic genitive of σύ, here a genitive of comparison, ‘than you’. οὔ τις ἀνήρ … μακάρτατος is ‘no man most blessed’ (μακάρτατος the superlative of μάκαρ ‘blessed’), with προπάροιθε ‘before’ and ὀπίσσω ‘after’. The Greek has no verb; the English supplies ‘has been’ and ‘will be’.

sentences.t:
πρὶν μὲν γάρ σε ζωὸν ἐτίομεν ἶσα θεοῖσιν
Ἀργεῖοι, νῦν αὖτε μέγα κρατέεις νεκύεσσιν
ἐνθάδ’ ἐών·
sentences.i: For before, when you were alive, we Argives honoured you equally with the gods, and now, being here, you have great power among the dead;
sentences.n: Why Achilles should not grieve: honoured in life, he rules among the dead. πρὶν μέν is ‘before’, ζωόν ‘living’ (a predicate accusative, ‘you alive’), ἐτίομεν ‘we honoured’ (imperfect of τίω), and ἶσα θεοῖσιν ‘equally with gods’, ἶσα being an adverb. Ἀργεῖοι is ‘Argives’, here the Greeks of the army generally. νῦν αὖτε μέγα κρατέεις νεκύεσσιν is ‘now again you hold great sway among the dead’: κρατέεις is the uncontracted form of κρατεῖς, from κρατέω ‘be strong, have power’, and νεκύεσσιν the -εσσι dative of νεκύς ‘dead man’. ἐνθάδ’ ἐών is ‘being here’. The ano teleia ends the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t: τῷ μή τι θανὼν ἀκαχίζευ, Ἀχιλλεῦ.
sentences.l: therefore do not at all, having died, grieve, Achilles.’
sentences.i: so do not grieve at all at being dead, Achilles.’
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘therefore’; μή τι … ἀκαχίζευ is ‘do not grieve at all’ (ἀκαχίζομαι ‘grieve’, an imperative in -ευ), with θανών the aorist participle of θνῄσκω, ‘having died’. Odysseus’ speech ends.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δέ μ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπε·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and he then at once, answering me, addressed me:
sentences.i: So I said, and he answered me at once:
sentences.n: Achilles’ reply-formula, the same line as 11.404 and 11.440, with the same English as shipped.

sentences.t: μὴ δή μοι θάνατόν γε παραύδα, φαίδιμ’ Ὀδυσσεῦ.
sentences.l: ‘Not, now, to me of death at least speak soothingly, glorious Odysseus.
sentences.i: ‘Do not try, glorious Odysseus, to soothe me about death.
sentences.n: Achilles’ answer. μὴ δή μοι θάνατόν γε παραύδα is ‘do not now, to me, speak soothingly of death’: παραυδάω is ‘speak to, talk round, console’ (παρά ‘beside’ and αὐδάω ‘speak’), μή with the imperative forbids, and θάνατον is the thing he is not to console him about. φαίδιμ’ Ὀδυσσεῦ is ‘glorious Odysseus’, with ‘glorious’ the house word for φαίδιμος.

sentences.t:
βουλοίμην κ’ ἐπάρουρος ἐὼν θητευέμεν ἄλλῳ,
ἀνδρὶ παρ’ ἀκλήρῳ, ᾧ μὴ βίοτος πολὺς εἴη,
ἢ πᾶσιν νεκύεσσι καταφθιμένοισιν ἀνάσσειν.
sentences.l:
I would wish, being on the ploughland, to work for hire for another,
with a man without allotment, to whom there would not be much livelihood,
rather than over all the dead who have perished to be lord.
sentences.i: I would rather work on the land as another man’s hired hand, a landless man who has little to live on, than be lord over all the dead who have perished.
sentences.n: The famous preference. βουλοίμην κ’ is ‘I would wish’, an optative with κε, a potential statement. ἐπάρουρος ἐών is ‘being on the ploughland’ (ἐπί and ἄρουρα ‘ploughed field’); the exact force of ἐπάρουρος, whether ‘alive on the earth’ or ‘tied to the soil’, is not certain. θητευέμεν is the infinitive of θητεύω ‘work for hire’ (θής ‘hired labourer’), ἀνδρὶ παρ’ ἀκλήρῳ ‘with a man without an allotment’ (ἄκληρος: no κλῆρος, ‘lot, plot of land’), and ᾧ μὴ βίοτος πολὺς εἴη ‘to whom there might not be much livelihood’, a relative clause with the optative that describes the kind of man. ἢ … ἀνάσσειν is ‘rather than to be lord over’ (ἀνάσσω ‘be lord’, from ἄναξ), with πᾶσιν νεκύεσσι καταφθιμένοισιν ‘all the dead who have perished’ (the aorist participle of καταφθίνω).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τοῦ παιδὸς ἀγαυοῦ μῦθον ἐνίσπες,
ἢ ἕπετ’ ἐς πόλεμον πρόμος ἔμμεναι, ἦε καὶ οὐκί.
sentences.l:
But come, to me of the noble child the tale tell,
whether he followed into war to be a foremost fighter, or even not.
sentences.i: But come, tell me the tale of that noble son, whether he went to the war to be a foremost fighter, or not.
sentences.n: The question about his son. ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, and τοῦ παιδὸς ἀγαυοῦ is ‘of that noble child’: τοῦ is a demonstrative pointing at Neoptolemus, whom Achilles does not name here. μῦθον ἐνίσπες is ‘tell the tale’ (ἐνίσπες the aorist imperative of ἐνέπω). ἢ … ἦε καὶ οὐκί is ‘whether … or not’: ἕπετ’ is the unaugmented ἕπετο ‘followed’, πρόμος ‘foremost fighter’, and ἔμμεναι the infinitive ‘to be’ (= εἶναι). The Greek says only that he ‘followed into the war’ and does not say whom he followed.

sentences.t:
εἰπὲ δέ μοι Πηλῆος ἀμύμονος, εἴ τι πέπυσσαι,
ἢ ἔτ’ ἔχει τιμὴν πολέσιν μετὰ Μυρμιδόνεσσιν,
ἦ μιν ἀτιμάζουσιν ἀν’ Ἑλλάδα τε Φθίην τε,
οὕνεκά μιν κατὰ γῆρας ἔχει χεῖράς τε πόδας τε.
sentences.l:
And tell me of blameless Peleus, whether you have learned anything,
whether he still holds honour among the many Myrmidons,
or whether they dishonour him throughout Hellas and Phthia,
because old age has hold of him in hands and feet.
sentences.i: And tell me of blameless Peleus, if you have learned anything: whether he still holds honour among the many Myrmidons, or whether they dishonour him throughout Hellas and Phthia, because old age grips him in hands and feet.
sentences.n: And about his father. εἰπὲ δέ μοι is ‘and tell me’, and εἴ τι πέπυσσαι ‘if you have learned anything’ (πέπυσσαι perfect of πυνθάνομαι). Πηλῆος ἀμύμονος is ‘of blameless Peleus’, ἀμύμων being rendered ‘blameless’ whatever its true sense. Then two alternatives, ἢ … ἦ ‘whether … or whether’: τιμὴν ἔχει ‘he holds honour’, πολέσιν … Μυρμιδόνεσσιν ‘among the many Myrmidons’ (πολέσιν the epic dative plural of πολύς), and ἀτιμάζουσιν ‘they dishonour’. ἀν’ Ἑλλάδα τε Φθίην τε is ‘up and down Hellas and Phthia’, two districts of the same region, so Hellas is not yet the whole of Greece. οὕνεκα is ‘because’, and κατὰ … ἔχει is a tmesis, ‘holds down’: old age (γῆρας) has him χεῖράς τε πόδας τε ‘in hands and feet’, accusatives of respect.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐγὼν ἐπαρωγὸς ὑπ’ αὐγὰς ἠελίοιο,
τοῖος ἐών, οἷός ποτ’ ἐνὶ Τροίῃ εὐρείῃ
πέφνον λαὸν ἄριστον, ἀμύνων Ἀργείοισιν·
sentences.i: for I am no helper to him under the rays of the sun, not being such as I once was in broad Troy, when I killed the best of the host, defending the Argives;
sentences.n: Achilles’ wish to help his father. οὐ γὰρ ἐγών … ἐπαρωγός is ‘for I am not a helper’ (ἐπαρωγός ‘one who comes to help’), and ὑπ’ αὐγὰς ἠελίοιο is ‘under the rays of the sun’, that is, among the living. τοῖος ἐών, οἷος … is ‘being such as …’, with the negative of the main clause still in force, and πέφνον is again the unaugmented aorist ‘I killed’. Τροίῃ εὐρείῃ is ‘broad Troy’, and ἀμύνων Ἀργείοισιν ‘defending the Argives’. λαὸν ἄριστον is literally ‘the best people’ and is taken as the best of the host; the Greek does not say whose host. The English adds ‘to him’ after ‘helper’, which the sense requires.

sentences.t: εἰ τοιόσδ’ ἔλθοιμι μίνυνθά περ ἐς πατέρος δῶ·
sentences.l: if such I might come, even for a little while, to my father’s house;
sentences.i: if I could come, even for a little while, to my father’s house such as I was then;
sentences.n: The wish itself. εἰ τοιόσδ’ ἔλθοιμι is ‘if I could come as such a man’ (εἰ with the optative expresses a wish; τοιόσδε ‘such as this’ points back to the man he once was), μίνυνθά περ ‘even for a little while’, and ἐς πατέρος δῶ ‘to my father’s house’, with δῶ a short form of δῶμα ‘house’. The ano teleia ends the unit before the result.

sentences.t:
τῷ κέ τεῳ στύξαιμι μένος καὶ χεῖρας ἀάπτους,
οἳ κεῖνον βιόωνται ἐέργουσίν τ’ ἀπὸ τιμῆς.
sentences.l:
then to any I would make hateful my strength and hands untouchable,
who use force on him and keep him from honour.
sentences.i: then I would make my strength and my irresistible hands dreaded by any who use force on him and keep him from his honour.
sentences.n: The result. τῷ is ‘then’, and τεῳ is a form of τινί ‘to some one’, standing for ‘any of those who’ in the relative clause that follows. στύξαιμι is the aorist optative of στύζω, from the root of στυγέω ‘hate’, ‘make hateful, make shudder’, so the sense is ‘I would make my strength hateful, dreaded, to them’. The meaning of ἀάπτους in μένος καὶ χεῖρας ἀάπτους is not known; ‘untouchable’ and ‘irresistible’ are the traditional guesses, and the English gives one in each layer. οἳ κεῖνον βιόωνται ἐέργουσίν τ’ ἀπὸ τιμῆς is ‘who use force on him and keep him from honour’: βιόωνται is βιῶνται (βιάομαι ‘use force on’) in its uncontracted epic form, and ἐέργουσιν is the epic form of εἴργουσιν ‘shut out, keep away’. Achilles’ speech ends.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
sentences.n: The formula, here before Odysseus’ reply to Achilles. The English is kept exactly as when this line was shipped before, where the speaker was a woman; μιν is ‘him’ or ‘her’ in Greek, so read ‘she … her’ as ‘he … him’, for Achilles is the speaker.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι μὲν Πηλῆος ἀμύμονος οὔ τι πέπυσμαι,
αὐτάρ τοι παιδός γε Νεοπτολέμοιο φίλοιο
πᾶσαν ἀληθείην μυθήσομαι, ὥς με κελεύεις·
sentences.i: ‘Of blameless Peleus I have learned nothing; but of your dear son Neoptolemus I will tell you the whole truth, as you bid me;
sentences.n: Odysseus answers the two questions in turn. ἦ τοι μέν is ‘truly, indeed’, and Πηλῆος ἀμύμονος οὔ τι πέπυσμαι is ‘of blameless Peleus I have learned nothing’ (πέπυσμαι is the perfect of πυνθάνομαι, here with the genitive of the person asked about). αὐτάρ τοι begins the contrast, ‘but, I tell you’. παιδός γε Νεοπτολέμοιο φίλοιο is ‘of the child, dear Neoptolemus’, the name appearing for the first time in this part and the Greek having no ‘your’ with it; πᾶσαν ἀληθείην μυθήσομαι is ‘I will tell the whole truth’ (ἀληθείη ‘truth’), ὥς με κελεύεις ‘as you bid me’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς γάρ μιν ἐγὼ κοίλης ἐπὶ νηὸς ἐίσης
ἤγαγον ἐκ Σκύρου μετ’ ἐυκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
for I myself, on a hollow, well-balanced ship,
brought him from Scyros to the well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.i: For I myself brought him from Scyros on a hollow, well-balanced ship, to join the well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.n: How Odysseus knows. αὐτὸς γάρ … ἐγώ is ‘for I myself’, ἤγαγον ‘I brought’, and ἐκ Σκύρου ‘from Scyros’, an island. κοίλης ἐπὶ νηὸς ἐίσης is ‘on a hollow, well-balanced ship’: ἐίσης is rendered ‘well-balanced’ in the house, though the sense of the word is uncertain. μετ’ ἐυκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς is ‘to join the well-greaved Achaeans’ (μετά with the accusative, ‘into the midst of’; ἐυκνήμιδες ‘with fine greaves’, greaves being shin-guards).

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι ὅτ’ ἀμφὶ πόλιν Τροίην φραζοίμεθα βουλάς,
αἰεὶ πρῶτος ἔβαζε καὶ οὐχ ἡμάρτανε μύθων·
sentences.l:
Truly, whenever about the city, Troy, we would devise plans,
always first he would speak and not miss in his words;
sentences.i: Whenever we took counsel about the city of Troy, he would always speak first, and never missed the mark in what he said;
sentences.n: Neoptolemus in counsel. ἦ τοι ὅτ’ … φραζοίμεθα βουλάς is ‘whenever we would take counsel’: ὅτε with the optative makes the occasion repeated, φραζοίμεθα is the optative of φράζομαι ‘consider, plan’, and ἀμφὶ πόλιν Τροίην is ‘about the city of Troy’. αἰεὶ πρῶτος ἔβαζε is ‘he always spoke first’ (ἔβαζε the imperfect of βάζω, as in βάζειν above), and οὐχ ἡμάρτανε μύθων ‘he did not miss in his words’ (ἁμαρτάνω with the genitive). The subject, ‘he’, is Neoptolemus.

sentences.t: Νέστωρ ἀντίθεος καὶ ἐγὼ νικάσκομεν οἴω.
sentences.l: Nestor, godlike, and I, we two alone, used to surpass him.
sentences.i: Only godlike Nestor and I used to better him.
sentences.n: Νέστωρ ἀντίθεος is ‘godlike Nestor’, with ‘godlike’ the house word for ἀντίθεος; ἐγώ is Odysseus. νικάσκομεν is the iterative ‘we used to win, be better’, and οἴω is the dual ‘we two alone’. The Greek does not say who was beaten, and ‘him’ (Neoptolemus) is supplied from the line before.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅτ’ ἐν πεδίῳ Τρώων μαρναίμεθα χαλκῷ,
οὔ ποτ’ ἐνὶ πληθυῖ μένεν ἀνδρῶν οὐδ’ ἐν ὁμίλῳ,
ἀλλὰ πολὺ προθέεσκε τὸ ὃν μένος οὐδενὶ εἴκων,
πολλοὺς δ’ ἄνδρας ἔπεφνεν ἐν αἰνῇ δηιοτῆτι.
sentences.l:
But whenever on the plain of the Trojans we would fight with bronze,
never in the throng of men would he stay, nor in the crowd,
but far ahead he would run, his own strength to no one yielding,
and many men he killed in fearsome fighting.
sentences.i: But whenever we fought with bronze on the plain of the Trojans, he never stayed in the throng or the crowd of men, but ran far out ahead, yielding in his strength to no one, and killed many men in fearsome fighting.
sentences.n: Neoptolemus in battle. ὅτ’ … μαρναίμεθα is again ‘whenever we fought’ (the optative of μάρναμαι ‘fight’), ἐν πεδίῳ Τρώων ‘on the plain of the Trojans’, and χαλκῷ ‘with bronze’. μένεν is the unaugmented imperfect ‘he stayed’, πληθυῖ the dative of πληθύς ‘throng’, and ὁμίλῳ ‘crowd’. προθέεσκε is the iterative ‘he would run out in front’ (πρό and θέω ‘run’). τὸ ὃν μένος is ‘his own strength’: τό is the article as a pronoun, and ὅν the possessive ‘his own’, easy to mistake for the relative. οὐδενὶ εἴκων is ‘yielding to no one’. ἐν αἰνῇ δηιοτῆτι is ‘in fearsome fighting’ (αἰνός, the house ‘fearsome’; δηιοτής ‘fighting, slaughter’).

sentences.t:
πάντας δ’ οὐκ ἂν ἐγὼ μυθήσομαι οὐδ’ ὀνομήνω,
ὅσσον λαὸν ἔπεφνεν ἀμύνων Ἀργείοισιν,
ἀλλ’ οἷον τὸν Τηλεφίδην κατενήρατο χαλκῷ,
ἥρω’ Εὐρύπυλον,
sentences.l:
But all I could not tell, nor name,
how great a host he killed, defending the Argives,
but what a man, the son of Telephus, he slew with bronze,
the hero Eurypylus,
sentences.i: I could not tell or name them all, however great a host he killed while defending the Argives; but what a man he killed with bronze in the son of Telephus, the hero Eurypylus,
sentences.n: The one he will name. πάντας … οὐκ ἂν … μυθήσομαι οὐδ’ ὀνομήνω is ‘I could not tell nor name them all’, with the potential sense ‘I could not’, and ὅσσον λαὸν ‘how great a host’. ἀλλ’ οἷον τὸν Τηλεφίδην κατενήρατο is ‘but what a man the son of Telephus (was) whom he killed’: οἷον is ‘what a (man)’, Τηλεφίδης the patronymic from Telephus, and κατενήρατο the aorist middle of κατεναίρω ‘kill’; ἥρω’ Εὐρύπυλον, ‘the hero Eurypylus’, is the name in apposition. The whole sentence would run five lines to its full stop, so it is cut at the comma after Εὐρύπυλον, where the syntax pauses.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ δ’ ἀμφ’ αὐτὸν ἑταῖροι
Κήτειοι κτείνοντο γυναίων εἵνεκα δώρων.
sentences.l:
and many around him, companions,
Ceteians, were being killed for the sake of women’s gifts.
sentences.i: and many of his Ceteian companions were killed around him, for the sake of women’s gifts.
sentences.n: The end of the sentence. πολλοὶ δ’ ἀμφ’ αὐτὸν ἑταῖροι Κήτειοι is ‘and many companions around him, Ceteians’: the Ceteians are a people, and who they were is not known. κτείνοντο is the imperfect passive of κτείνω ‘were being killed’, and γυναίων εἵνεκα δώρων ‘for the sake of women’s gifts’: γυναῖος is an adjective, ‘of women’, and the Greek does not say whether the gifts were given to a woman or by one, so the English keeps ‘women’s’.

sentences.t: κεῖνον δὴ κάλλιστον ἴδον μετὰ Μέμνονα δῖον.
sentences.l: That one, indeed, the most beautiful I saw, after heavenly Memnon.
sentences.i: He was the most beautiful man I saw, after heavenly Memnon.
sentences.n: The praise of his looks. ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω ‘I saw’, with κεῖνον … κάλλιστον ‘that one the most beautiful’, and μετὰ Μέμνονα δῖον is ‘after heavenly Memnon’: μετά with the accusative ‘next after’, and δῖος the house ‘heavenly’. Memnon is only named in these lines and is not described.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅτ’ εἰς ἵππον κατεβαίνομεν, ὃν κάμ’ Ἐπειός,
Ἀργείων οἱ ἄριστοι, ἐμοὶ δ’ ἐπὶ πάντα τέταλτο,
ἠμὲν ἀνακλῖναι πυκινὸν λόχον ἠδ’ ἐπιθεῖναι,
sentences.l:
But when into the horse we were going down, which Epeius made,
we the best of the Argives, and to me everything was entrusted,
both to open and to shut the solid ambush,
sentences.i: But when we, the best of the Argives, went down into the horse that Epeius made, and everything was entrusted to me, both to open and to shut the solid ambush,
sentences.n: The wooden horse. κατεβαίνομεν is ‘we were going down’ (imperfect of καταβαίνω), εἰς ἵππον ‘into the horse’, and ὃν κάμ’ Ἐπειός ‘that Epeius made’ (κάμ’ = ἔκαμε, the aorist of κάμνω ‘toil, make with labour’). Ἀργείων οἱ ἄριστοι is ‘the best of the Argives’, in apposition to the ‘we’. ἐμοὶ δ’ ἐπὶ πάντα τέταλτο is ‘and everything was entrusted to me’: τέταλτο is the pluperfect passive of ἐπιτέλλω ‘lay upon, enjoin’, with ἐπί separated. ἠμὲν … ἠδ’ is ‘both … and’; ἀνακλῖναι is ‘to lay back, open’ and ἐπιθεῖναι ‘to put to, shut’, and the object πυκινὸν λόχον is ‘the solid ambush’, the men packed in the horse (πυκινός ‘dense, solid’, λόχος ‘ambush’). The Greek does not mention a door; ‘open and shut’ is what the two verbs say. The five-line sentence is cut at this comma.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄλλοι Δαναῶν ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες
δάκρυά τ’ ὠμόργνυντο τρέμον θ’ ὑπὸ γυῖα ἑκάστου·
sentences.l:
then the other leaders and lords of the Danaans
tears wiped away, and trembled beneath each man his limbs;
sentences.i: then the other leaders and lords of the Greeks wiped away their tears, and each man’s limbs trembled beneath him;
sentences.n: The Greek leaders weep and shake. ἔνθ’ is ‘then, there’, and ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες ‘leaders and lords’, as of the Phaeacians elsewhere, here of the Danaans (the literal layer says ‘Danaans’, the other ‘Greeks’). δάκρυά τ’ ὠμόργνυντο is ‘and wiped away tears’ (the imperfect middle of ὀμόργνυμι), and τρέμον θ’ … γυῖα ἑκάστου ‘and each man’s limbs trembled’, with τρέμον the unaugmented imperfect and ὑπό ‘beneath’. The ano teleia ends the unit.

sentences.t:
κεῖνον δ’ οὔ ποτε πάμπαν ἐγὼν ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσιν
οὔτ’ ὠχρήσαντα χρόα κάλλιμον οὔτε παρειῶν
δάκρυ ὀμορξάμενον·
sentences.i: But I never once saw him with my own eyes turn pale in his fair skin, or wipe a tear from his cheeks;
sentences.n: Neoptolemus did not weep. κεῖνον δ’ is ‘but that one’, οὔ ποτε πάμπαν ‘never at all’, and ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ‘I saw with my eyes’, a stock way of saying ‘I saw it myself’. ὠχρήσαντα is the aorist participle of ὠχράω ‘turn pale’, with χρόα κάλλιμον ‘in his fair skin’ (an accusative of respect; the house ‘fair’ for κάλλιμος), and οὔτε παρειῶν δάκρυ ὀμορξάμενον ‘nor wiping a tear from his cheeks’: the verb is the one in ὠμόργνυντο, with the genitive παρειῶν ‘from the cheeks’. The ano teleia ends the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ὁ δέ γε μάλα πόλλ’ ἱκέτευεν
ἱππόθεν ἐξέμεναι, ξίφεος δ’ ἐπεμαίετο κώπην
καὶ δόρυ χαλκοβαρές, κακὰ δὲ Τρώεσσι μενοίνα.
sentences.l:
but he very much kept begging
out of the horse to be let out, and for his sword’s hilt kept feeling
and for his bronze-heavy spear, and evils for the Trojans he was eager for.
sentences.i: but he begged very hard to be let out of the horse, and kept feeling for the hilt of his sword and for his bronze-heavy spear, and was eager to do harm to the Trojans.
sentences.n: What he did instead. ὁ δέ γε is ‘but he’, and μάλα πόλλ’ ἱκέτευεν ‘kept begging very much’. ἱππόθεν is ‘out of the horse’ (the -θεν of source), and ἐξέμεναι an infinitive of ἐξίημι ‘let go out’, ‘to be let out’; no subject is stated, so ‘to go out’ is also possible. ξίφεος δ’ ἐπεμαίετο κώπην is ‘and kept feeling for the hilt of his sword’: ἐπιμαίομαι ‘feel over, reach for’ takes the genitive, and κώπη is ‘hilt’. δόρυ χαλκοβαρές is ‘his bronze-heavy spear’: χαλκοβαρής is ‘heavy with bronze’ (χαλκός and βαρύς), most likely a heavy bronze head. κακὰ δὲ Τρώεσσι μενοίνα is ‘and he was eager for evils for the Trojans’ (μενοινάω ‘be eager, intend’).

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ Πριάμοιο πόλιν διεπέρσαμεν αἰπήν,
sentences.l: But when indeed Priam’s city, steep, we had sacked,
sentences.i: But when we had sacked the steep city of Priam,
sentences.n: The ending. ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ is ‘but when’, Πριάμοιο πόλιν … αἰπήν is ‘the steep city of Priam’ (αἰπύς ‘steep’, said here of a city on a height), and διεπέρσαμεν is the aorist of διαπέρθω ‘sack utterly’. The sentence runs through the end of line 537 and would be five lines long, so the unit is cut at this comma, where the subordinate clause is complete and the main clause begins.

sentences.t:
μοῖραν καὶ γέρας ἐσθλὸν ἔχων ἐπὶ νηὸς ἔβαινεν
ἀσκηθής, οὔτ’ ἂρ βεβλημένος ὀξέι χαλκῷ
οὔτ’ αὐτοσχεδίην οὐτασμένος, οἷά τε πολλὰ
γίγνεται ἐν πολέμῳ·
sentences.l:
a portion and a good prize holding, he went onto the ship,
unscathed, neither struck by sharp bronze
nor wounded at close quarters, such as many
happen in war;
sentences.i: he went aboard his ship with his portion and a good prize, unscathed, neither struck by sharp bronze nor wounded in close combat, as so often happens in war;
sentences.n: What he took and how he came through. μοῖραν καὶ γέρας ἐσθλόν is ‘a portion and a good prize’, his share of the spoils, and ἔχων ἐπὶ νηὸς ἔβαινεν ‘holding (them) he went aboard the ship’. ἀσκηθής is ‘unscathed’, and the two οὔτε clauses say how: βεβλημένος ὀξέι χαλκῷ ‘struck by sharp bronze’ (βάλλω is ‘hit with something thrown or shot’), αὐτοσχεδίην οὐτασμένος ‘wounded hand to hand’ (an adverbial accusative; οὐτάω is ‘wound with a thrust’). οἷά τε πολλὰ γίγνεται ἐν πολέμῳ is literally ‘such as many happen in war’, with τε marking a general truth. The ano teleia ends the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t: ἐπιμὶξ δέ τε μαίνεται Ἄρης.
sentences.l: and in confusion rages Ares.’
sentences.i: and Ares rages in confusion.’
sentences.n: ἐπιμίξ is ‘in a mixture, in confusion, without order’ (from the root of μίγνυμι ‘mix’; the word is rare), and μαίνεται ‘rages’ (μαίνομαι ‘be mad, rave’). Ἄρης is the god of war and also war’s fury, and δέ τε marks a general truth, here the reason wounds come without choosing their man. Odysseus’ speech to Achilles ends; the larger tale he is telling the Phaeacians goes on.
